extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, journalism students, newsroom editors and professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and applying a taxonomy of news values to explain why particular items are selected as news in mainstream media and online (including social media shareability). The article empirically tests and updates Harcup & O'Neill's 2001 list using UK newspaper and social-media data from 2014.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power elite (NV1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning powerful individuals, organisations or institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as one of the original Harcup & O'Neill (2001) news values; more significant in broadsheet/quality press where 'serious' news is prominent. The authors note corporations often appear in this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity (NV2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning people who are already famous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in red-top papers; O'Neill (2012) suggests a hierarchy may exist with celebrity dominating in some outlets. Also relevant to online sharing cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment (NV3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning sex, showbusiness, human interest, animals, an unfolding drama, or offering opportunities for humorous treatment, entertaining photographs or witty headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third biggest news value in the 2014 newspaper sample; authors argue the category can be subdivided (e.g. drama, sport, showbusiness) and that entertainment stories are especially prominent in popular/tabloid titles and online share metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise / Unusualness (NV4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that have an element of surprise and/or contrast (including unusualness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranks highly in empirical findings; authors suggest ‘surprise’ should explicitly include 'unusualness' in its definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news (NV5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly negative overtones, such as conflict or tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most frequent news value in the 2014 sample. Authors note that some stories can be both bad and good news depending on viewpoint; Phillips (2015) argues conflict should be split out from bad news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good news (NV6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly positive overtones, such as rescues and cures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less frequent than bad news but still significant; stories can simultaneously contain good and bad elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (NV7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are perceived as sufficiently significant either in the numbers of people involved or in potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue 'magnitude' should be broadened to include extremes of behaviour or occurrences (e.g. extraordinarily unpleasant crimes, extreme death circumstances) as well as sheer numbers/impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance (NV8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about issues, groups and nations perceived to be relevant to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A core Harcup & O'Neill value; in local news 'proximity' is a strong form of relevance (e.g. local stories dominated by proximity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up (NV9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about subjects already in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognises seriality in coverage and the newsworthiness of continuing developments; coding in the study specifically marked follow-up items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper agenda (NV10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that set or fit the news organisation’s own agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed more in mid-market titles in the sample; can include overt editorial framing and selective emphasis consistent with a paper's stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict (proposed separate value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories featuring conflict as the central newsworthiness driver (distinct from the broader 'bad news' category).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phillips (2015) and the authors suggest teasing conflict out as its own category rather than subsuming it under bad news because conflict is a dominant determinant of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity / Being first
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories for which the outlet has exclusive access, scoops, investigations or is first to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors found frequent explicit claims of exclusivity (e.g. 'an investigation by...' or 'a poll by...') and argue exclusivity merits recognition as its own news value because being first or exclusive often overrides other values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visuals / Strong imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of strong photographs, design or visual elements that emphasise and convey news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caple & Bednarek (2015) and the authors note visuals can be a direct reason for selection and can amplify values like drama, surprise, or bad news; visual appeal is important especially for online/social sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability / Sociability
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a story is likely to be shared on social media platforms (e.g. Facebook, Twitter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as an emergent news value: stories that 'make you laugh' or 'make you angry' tend to be widely shared. Facebook favors accessible, entertainment/lifestyle content; Twitter favors serious news brands. Audience metrics (clicks/shares) can influence journalists' selection/prioritisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Being current, breaking or topical (the news is new or immediate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schultz (2007) lists timeliness as a dominant news value; being first (exclusivity) and topicality often override other considerations in a competitive environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification / Proximity to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that allow audiences to identify with the people, places or situations described (including geographical proximity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schultz includes identification as a dominant value; local proximity was shown empirically to be a top factor in local news consumption (e.g. 76% proximity in one local sample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation / Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories emphasising sensational, shocking or emotionally intense elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schultz and Allern highlight sensation as a driver; related to commercial news values where sensational stories are more likely to be pursued for audience appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial news values / Cost and audience appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection biased by commercial considerations: sensationalism, low-cost-to-pursue stories, and appeal to target audiences (clickability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allern's supplementary set: news organisations pursue sensational stories, avoid costly investigations, and favour prepared news subsidies (press releases/photo ops); audience clicks and commercial targets influence selection especially online.

rubrics_metrics.name: News subsidies / Prefabrication (PR influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories supplied or made easier to produce by prepared press releases, photo opportunities, or PR resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bell (1991) calls this prefabrication; Lewis et al. (2008) observed such subsidies are more readily used by resource-strapped newsrooms, affecting selection and coverage frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition / Expectation / Worth / External influences (Brighton & Foy factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of selection considerations proposed by Brighton & Foy: Relevance; Topicality; Composition; Expectation; Unusualness; Worth; External influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brighton & Foy (2007) argue times and media have changed and propose these as factors to consider when selecting/analyzing news; they also note news values vary by medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-generated content / Participatory contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of audience-produced material (UGC) in selection and dissemination of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domingo et al. (2008) and others show UGC affects what audiences receive; participatory journalism more common in online/tabloid contexts and can influence both selection and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-specific affordances (Facebook vs Twitter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform differences that shape what is selected to attract attention: Facebook favors accessible/entertainment content; Twitter favors serious brands and hard news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman (2015) and the authors summarise evidence that different social platforms privilege different content types, influencing newsroom decisions aiming for traffic or engagement.
